title: Long-Running Transactions
description: Learn why long-running transactions are dangerous in SQL Server, how they cause log growth, blocking, and replication lag, and how to detect and fix them.

data.text: A **long-running transaction** is any transaction that stays open for an extended period — from a few seconds to hours or even days. In SQL Server, an open transaction does more than hold locks. It prevents the transaction log from being truncated, blocks log backups, causes replication or Always On delays, and can fill the transaction log until the database runs out of space.

Long-running transactions are not always obvious. A transaction can be open because a developer forgot to commit it, because an application is waiting for user input inside a transaction, or because a batch job is processing millions of rows in a single transaction. In all cases, the consequences for the production database are the same: instability.

data.title: Consequences of Long-Running Transactions
items: Transaction log cannot be truncated — the log must contain every change from the oldest open transaction (the Virtual Log Files containing that transaction's changes cannot be reused)
Log backups cannot truncate the log — if your recovery model is FULL or BULK_LOGGED, log backups fail to free space, and the log file grows until it fills the disk
Blocking cascades — locks held by the long transaction block other sessions, which may queue up behind it
Replication and Always On latency — the long transaction must complete before changes can be sent to replicas or Availability Group secondaries
Tempdb pressure — large rollback segments and version store growth from concurrent snapshot queries

data.text: SQL Server exposes open transaction information through Dynamic Management Views. The key view is `sys.dm_tran_active_transactions`, which shows all active transactions, their state, and how long they have been running. You can combine it with `sys.dm_tran_database_transactions` and `sys.dm_exec_sessions` to identify the exact session and SQL causing the problem.

data.title: Find Long-Running Transactions
data.content: Query active transactions and calculate their age.
data.code:
SELECT 
    at.transaction_id,
    at.name AS transaction_name,
    at.transaction_begin_time,
    DATEDIFF(SECOND, at.transaction_begin_time, GETDATE()) AS elapsed_seconds,
    at.transaction_state,
    at.transaction_status,
    s.session_id,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    s.program_name,
    s.status AS session_status,
    SUBSTRING(st.text, (r.statement_start_offset/2)+1,
        ((CASE r.statement_end_offset
            WHEN -1 THEN DATALENGTH(st.text)
            ELSE r.statement_end_offset END
          - r.statement_start_offset)/2)+1) AS current_sql
FROM sys.dm_tran_active_transactions AS at
INNER JOIN sys.dm_tran_database_transactions AS dt ON at.transaction_id = dt.transaction_id
INNER JOIN sys.dm_tran_session_transactions AS st ON dt.transaction_id = st.transaction_id
INNER JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON st.session_id = s.session_id
LEFT OUTER JOIN sys.dm_exec_requests AS r ON s.session_id = r.session_id
OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS st_text
WHERE at.transaction_type = 1  -- user-initiated transaction
ORDER BY elapsed_seconds DESC;

data.title: Transaction State Codes
data.text: In sys.dm_tran_active_transactions, transaction_state = 1 means the transaction has not started, 2 means it is active, 3 means it is ending, and 4 means the commit has been initiated. A transaction stuck in state 2 for a long time is the one to investigate.

Long-running transactions usually have one of a few root causes. Identifying the cause is more important than killing the transaction — killing it causes a rollback that takes as long as the transaction took to run, and during that rollback the database remains blocked.

data.title: Root Causes and Remedies
items: Application waits inside a transaction — fix by moving user input, API calls, and computations outside the transaction; use the Unit of Work pattern
Batch jobs processing millions of rows — fix by breaking the batch into smaller chunks (e.g., 10,000 rows per transaction) and committing between chunks
Forgotten transactions — fix by adding transaction timeout logic or using SET LOCK_TIMEOUT to prevent indefinite waits
Blocking preventing commit — fix by resolving the blocking chain first; do not kill the long transaction if it is blocked by someone else
Snapshot isolation write conflicts — fix by retrying the transaction with exponential backoff

data.title: Never Kill Without a Plan
data.text: Killing a long-running transaction with KILL forces a rollback. The rollback runs at the same speed as the original transaction (sometimes slower), and during rollback the database holds locks and blocks other sessions. Use KILL only as a last resort, and warn stakeholders that the database will remain busy during rollback.

items.question: How long is too long for a transaction?
items.answer: For OLTP systems, aim for sub-second transactions. For batch workloads, keep individual transactions under a few minutes. Any transaction that runs longer than your log backup interval risks filling the transaction log.

items.question: Can I see who started a transaction?
items.answer: Yes. The DMV query above joins sys.dm_exec_sessions to show the login name, host name, program name, and current SQL for every active transaction. This usually points directly to the offending application or batch job.

items.question: Does READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT help with long transactions?
items.answer: RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking, which can reduce the side effects of long transactions. However, it does not fix the root problem: the open transaction still prevents log truncation and causes replication latency.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Long-running transactions prevent log truncation, cause log growth, block log backups, and delay replication
Detect them with sys.dm_tran_active_transactions joined to session and request DMVs
Killing a long transaction causes a rollback of equal duration — do not treat KILL as a quick fix
The real fix is architectural: move work outside transactions, batch in smaller chunks, and add timeouts
Transaction log size should be monitored alongside active transaction age as a pair of leading indicators
data.takeaway: The best long-running transaction is the one that never opens. Design your data access layer to keep transactions short, bounded, and explicit.
